terms.latin: famulus, famulī m.; famula, famulae f.
evidence: Cic. Off. 2.24: ut herīs in famulōs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The member of a household who serves (the word that gave familia). In Rome a house servant was normally a slave, so the classical words cover that too; for a slave as such, servus; for someone paid, see employee.

terms.gloss: attendant, servant who waits on someone
terms.comment: One who serves at hand: at table, at a sacrifice, in an office; then any helper or agent. Not a government minister classically (see minister).

evidence: Plaut. Mil. 3.1.199: ecqua ancilla est illī? (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The usual classical word for a woman servant, as the feminine of servus.

phrases.latin: dant famulī manibus lymphās Cereremque canistrīs expediunt
phrases.english: the servants pour water on their hands and serve bread from the baskets

phrases.latin: et clārā famulam poscit mortāria vōce
phrases.english: and he calls loudly to the maid for the mortar

sources: Lewis & Short: famulus · Lewis & Short: minister · Lewis & Short: ancilla · Lewis & Short: servus
Virgil and the Moretum from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-vergilius); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 167.
